summary: Zimbabwe sorts visitors into three lists: SADC neighbors and much of the Commonwealth Caribbean and Pacific enter visa-free, while most Western tourists — including US, UK, EU, Canadian and Australian passports — simply buy a visa on arrival from USD 30. A minority of nationalities must have an eVisa or embassy visa approved before travel.

notes: It is illegal to photograph government buildings, airports, military sites, police and the presidential motorcade.
Camouflage-pattern clothing is prohibited for civilians in Zimbabwe.
Drones may not be flown without prior authorization from the Civil Aviation Authority of Zimbabwe.

payments.text: The gold-backed ZiG (ZWG) is the official currency, but US dollars are legal tender and remain the practical currency for visitors. Bring small-denomination USD notes in good condition, as torn or old bills are often refused. Cards work in larger hotels and supermarkets, but networks are unreliable; cash is essential outside the cities.

safety.text: Most visits — especially to Victoria Falls and the main safari circuits — are trouble-free. Petty theft occurs in cities, cash and fuel shortages flare up periodically, police roadblocks are common on intercity roads, and demonstrations should be avoided.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Zimbabwe Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: The dry season from May to October brings the best game viewing and comfortable temperatures. Victoria Falls is at its thundering fullest from about February to May and at its lowest around November.

tips.text: Combining Victoria Falls with Zambia? Ask for the KAZA UniVisa (USD 50) on arrival — it covers unlimited crossings between Zimbabwe and Zambia for 30 days, plus day trips into Botswana through Kazungula.
Bring enough US dollars in cash: visa-on-arrival fees are payable only in USD, ATMs and card terminals are unreliable, and worn or older-series notes are frequently refused.

Check your visa category before flying. Category A passports need nothing and Category B buy a visa at the border, but Category C nationals will be refused boarding without a visa approved in advance via evisa.gov.zw.
Do not photograph government buildings, airports, bridges, military sites or police — arrests over "sensitive" photography do happen. Camouflage clothing is also illegal for civilians.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Zimbabwe?
faq.answer: Most tourists do, but it is straightforward: US, UK, EU, Canadian, Australian, Japanese and most other Western passports (Category B) buy a visa on arrival from USD 30. SADC neighbors and many Commonwealth countries (Category A) enter visa-free, while Category C nationalities must have a visa approved before travel via evisa.gov.zw or an embassy.

faq.question: How much is the Zimbabwe visa on arrival?
faq.answer: USD 30 single entry and USD 45 double entry for most Category B nationalities. British and Irish passport holders pay USD 55 for single entry, and Canadians pay USD 75. Bring the fee in US dollar cash — cards frequently fail at the border.

faq.question: What is the KAZA UniVisa?
faq.answer: A USD 50 joint visa covering both Zimbabwe and Zambia for 30 days with unlimited crossings between the two, plus day trips to Botswana's Chobe via Kazungula. It is sold on arrival at Victoria Falls and Harare airports and the main Zambezi land borders to most Category B nationalities — availability has lapsed before, so confirm it is on sale before relying on it.

faq.question: What currency should I bring to Zimbabwe?
faq.answer: US dollars in cash. The gold-backed ZiG is the official currency, but USD is legal tender and is what hotels, parks and border posts actually quote. Bring clean, small-denomination notes and expect change to be scarce.

faq.question: Can I extend my stay in Zimbabwe?
faq.answer: Yes — tourist entries are typically granted for 30 days and can be extended at Department of Immigration Control offices, usually in 30-day increments up to a maximum of about 90 days in total. Apply before your current stay expires.
